staged_source_snapshot.description: Stage 01 reproduced against this staged vulnerable checkout, so the line anchors below refer to this tree even though sample metadata names `2edbe2627697d07bf001b8cfa48f314fb6dbc47e` as the vulnerable commit.

classification.classification_note: The immediate sanitizer symptom is a 1-byte stack read past the temporary `data` array in `glz::atoi`, caused by using an undersized 24-byte scratch buffer while parsing a 64-bit decimal value with exponent text.

bug_description.original: OSS-Fuzz issue 425725152 (glaze): Stack-buffer-overflow READ 1 found by fuzz target csv_parsing [asan]. https://issues.oss-fuzz.com/issues/425725152
bug_description.original_source: sample_info.json issue_description / reproduction_report.json / sanitizer_trace.txt / default_crash_trace.txt / patch.diff / exact staged vulnerable source / exact staged `poc` bytes
bug_description.normalized: Stage 01 reproduced the saved ASan crash against the staged Glaze checkout at `d4d6ee98081a6f16198eaed8a967867a1da8dd97`, so the line anchors below refer to that tree. The exact witness `gt_results/arvo_425725152/poc` is a 76-byte raw file (sha256 `346b29497f066b8bd31e73e9a00eb184c55342109cab4c2dec7f81b3ac1c31ff`) whose first line is the 4-byte header cell `20 10 8f 00` and whose second line is the 60-byte decimal string `10678884521321086996e+113724712049423.1452152B321086996e-911`. In column-wise CSV mode, `read_column_wise_keys()` materializes that 4-byte header and `decode_hash_with_size<CSV, my_struct, ...>` maps it to member index 2, so parsing continues into `my_struct::maybe` (`std::vector<bool>`). The bool reader then treats the second line as a `uint64_t` by calling `glz::atoi(temp, it, end)`. For 64-bit integers the vulnerable tree uses `int_buffer_lengths[3] == 24`, so the outer `atoi` copies only the first 24 bytes `10678884521321086996e+11` into a 24-byte stack buffer and runs the inner parser on that truncated copy. `parse_int()` stops at the `'e'` after the 20-digit mantissa, the exponent handler consumes `+11`, and the third-exponent-digit probe at `atoi.hpp:394` dereferences `data + 24`, one byte past the copied buffer. This matches the saved AddressSanitizer `stack-buffer-overflow READ of size 1`, and the fix corroborates the missing obligation by increasing the 64-bit scratch-buffer entry from 24 to 32 with the comment `Increase by 8 to support exponentials`.

source.description: First project parser statement that materializes the attacker-controlled CSV header cell later hashed into the vulnerable `maybe` member dispatch.
source.value_from: The staged witness `gt_results/arvo_425725152/poc` begins with the exact bytes `20 10 8f 00 0a`. `read_column_wise_keys()` reads bytes 0..3 before the first newline into this `sv` header key.

relation.description: Source identity relation for the vulnerability-relevant value.

sink.description: AddressSanitizer sink. After the exponent parser advances `c` to one byte past the copied scratch buffer, this third-exponent-digit check reads `*c` out of bounds.
sink.note: The saved ASan trace reports frame #0 at `include/glaze/util/atoi.hpp:394:23`, `READ of size 1`, and names the overflowed inlined object as `data.i`.

root_cause.description: Root cause. For 64-bit parsing this statement selects `int_buffer_lengths[3] == 24`, so the wrapper allocates only a 24-byte stack buffer before delegating to the inner exponent parser.
root_cause.note: The staged patch changes the backing table from `{8, 8, 16, 24}` to `{16, 16, 24, 32}` explicitly to support exponential forms, preventing the copied 64-bit buffer from ending at `...e+11`.

tainted_value_origin.description: The selected `maybe` element is parsed numerically here. This statement forwards the attacker-controlled second-line cell into the vulnerable 64-bit integer parser.
tainted_value_origin.note: At this call site `it` points to the second line `10678884521321086996e+113724712049423.1452152B321086996e-911`, and `end` is the end of the full 76-byte witness.

parser_admitted.code: const auto keys = read_column_wise_keys(ctx, it, end);
parser_admitted.description: The input reaches the vulnerable column-wise object parser path here: `glz::read_csv<glz::colwise>` calls the column-wise `from<CSV, my_struct>::op`, which first splits the header row into key slices before member dispatch.

evidence_limitations: Stage 02 used the saved vulnerable reproduction only. The remediation claim is source-grounded by `patch.diff`; it did not execute a fixed build.

No runtime disambiguation was permitted for this sample (`run_flags.json` sets `runtime_disambiguation` to false). The index-2 dispatch into `my_struct::maybe` is therefore grounded by static evaluation of Glaze's key-hash logic plus the saved ASan stack frame `operator()<2ul>()`, not by fresh instrumentation.

fine_trace.note: Source. The first CSV line is a single 4-byte header cell, so this statement materializes `key == "\x20\x10\x8f\x00"` from witness bytes 0..3 before the first newline.

For `my_struct` keys `{"num1","num2","maybe","v3s"}`, Glaze's static `hash_info<T>` on this tree chooses the `unique_per_length` scheme. Length-4 keys use discriminator position 3, and static evaluation yields `HashInfo.seed == 14523965596842631817` with table slot 3 mapped to member index 2. Because the malformed header has `n == 4` and byte 3 is `0x00`, this dispatch resolves to field index 2 (`maybe`).
With `index == 2`, `visit<N>` instantiates `I == 2`, so `member` is `value.maybe`. The saved ASan stack contains `operator()<2ul>()` at this call site, which matches the static dispatch.
The `maybe` member is a `std::vector<bool>`, so parsing this column appends one new bit and immediately recurses on the resulting `std::__bit_reference`.

fine_trace.code:
uint64_t temp;
if (not glz::atoi(temp, it, end)) [[unlikely]] {
fine_trace.note: The boolean CSV reader treats the current cell as an unsigned integer. Here `it` points to the 60-byte second line `10678884521321086996e+113724712049423.1452152B321086996e-911`, and `end` is the end of the full 76-byte witness.

Root cause. For `uint64_t` / `unsigned long`, `int_buffer_lengths[3]` is 24 in the vulnerable tree, so this wrapper allocates a 24-byte stack buffer even though the remaining tail length `n` is 71 bytes. The fix increases the 64-bit table entry to 32.
Because `n < buffer_length` is false (`71 < 24`), only the first 24 bytes `10678884521321086996e+11` are copied into `data`. The inner parser then operates on this truncated 24-byte stack copy.

fine_trace.code:
if (auto ptr = parse_int(v, reinterpret_cast<const uint8_t*>(c))) [[likely]] {
   c = reinterpret_cast<const Char*>(ptr);
fine_trace.note: `parse_int()` consumes the 20-digit mantissa `10678884521321086996` and returns `ptr == start + 20`, so `c` now points at `data[20] == 'e'` inside the copied scratch buffer.

Because `data[20]` is `'e'`, the exponential branch is taken. The parser skips `'e'`, skips `'+'`, reads the two in-buffer exponent digits `'1'` and `'1'`, and advances `c` to `start + 24`, exactly one byte past the copied array.

Sink. Step 9 leaves `c == start + 24`, so this third-exponent-digit probe dereferences one byte past the 24-byte stack array `data.i`. That is the exact saved AddressSanitizer `READ of size 1` at `atoi.hpp:394`.

allocation_context.description: ASan's inlined frame dump says the invalid read is just past stack object `[32, 56) 'data.i'` in this caller frame. That object corresponds to the inlined 24-byte `std::array<char, buffer_length> data{}` from the outer `glz::atoi` wrapper.

cross_validation.root_cause_matches_allocation_context: Yes. ASan's `data.i` object is the same inlined scratch array created by the outer `glz::atoi` wrapper, and the root-cause step explains why that array is only 24 bytes wide for 64-bit exponential parsing in the vulnerable tree.
